ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a long, highly structured presentation style during formal talks and brief, conversational exchanges before and after them. Early chat is casual and fragmented, full of greetings, side comments, repetitions, and technical-check questions; participants often overlap lightly or respond with quick affirmations like “yeah,” “okay,” and laughter-like reactions. Speakers hedge frequently with “I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “you know,” and “I guess,” especially when speculating, while questions are often prefaced politely—“I have a quick question,” “this may be naive,” or “can I ask”—and then unfold into multi-part thoughts. The tone is collegial, informal, and supportive even in technical discussion: challenges are framed as extensions, clarifications, or curiosity rather than direct disagreement. Non-native or spontaneous speech patterns are prominent, including false starts, self-corrections, repeated words, unfinished clauses, and loosely connected follow-ups. Moderation is light but efficient, using brief transitions, acknowledgments, and invitations for more questions.

Meeting style for this meeting (polite_friction): Courteous but with real tension. People disagree in an indirect way: with a question, a hedge, a long pause, or 'let's take that offline'. Some disagreements are dropped rather than resolved. Nobody raises their voice.

research_problem: Understanding why a low-cost point-of-care blood test is adopted in some rural clinics and left in a drawer in others.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Njeri
speakers.background: Dr. Njeri is a biomedical engineer with 11 years of experience evaluating diagnostic devices in decentralized and resource-variable settings. Her work combines bench verification, environmental stress testing, field failure analysis, and review of service logs to understand how battery condition, heat exposure, storage practices, calibration, consumable compatibility, and maintenance affect assay performance. She has supported district laboratories and primary-care facilities in troubleshooting point-of-care analyzers, but has learned to distinguish a technically functional device from one that fits routine care.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She opens by asking whether variation in use is explained by reliability under actual clinic conditions: whether batteries can be charged, storage temperatures remain within specification, calibration is current, maintenance is available, and staff trust the assay results. She treats the device as a socio-technical artifact whose observed use may reflect both measurable performance and users' accumulated experience of its dependability, while deferring to colleagues on questions of authority, meaning, and service organization.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
speakers.background: Dr. Alvarez is a medical anthropologist with 14 years of ethnographic research experience in rural maternal health, diagnostic technologies, and frontline care work in East and Southern Africa. She uses participant observation, semi-structured interviews, case tracing, and institutional ethnography to examine how clinical categories travel through everyday practice. Her prior studies have focused on professional hierarchies, informal care networks, the moral stakes of triage, and how patients and health workers interpret test results when laboratory infrastructure is uneven.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She opens by asking how nurses, patients, clinic managers, and local decision-makers understand anemia and the blood test; who is socially and professionally authorized to perform, interpret, reserve, or withhold it; and how informal referral relationships shape its use. She is likely to argue that a device left in a drawer cannot be understood simply as non-adoption: it may be embedded in local judgments about risk, legitimacy, workload, patient expectations, and the practical consequences of producing a result that the clinic cannot act on.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Kwame Mensah
speakers.background: Dr. Mensah is a public health implementation researcher with 16 years of experience studying maternal and child health service delivery, diagnostic scale-up, and district health systems. He has led mixed-methods evaluations using routine screening registers, stock records, facility assessments, workflow mapping, and implementation indicators such as reach, fidelity, adoption, and sustainability. He has worked with ministries and district teams on integrating new tools into antenatal care rather than treating them as stand-alone interventions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He opens by asking how supply continuity, antenatal screening workflows, staffing patterns, community health worker links, and formal referral pathways affect routine implementation. He frames use as a property of a service-delivery system: a test may be available and technically sound yet remain peripheral if it disrupts patient flow, lacks reagents or follow-up capacity, competes with other priorities, or does not connect to referral and treatment pathways. He seeks a bridging question about how technical performance and upkeep, social organization and meanings, and health-system workflows jointly shape whether and how clinics incorporate the test into care, without presuming which domain is decisive.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

benchmark_task: Give a meeting with three disciplines, each opening with a different research question, that loosely converge on a shared question. The evaluated AI must capture the bridging question while preserving all three disciplinary sub-questions.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting with three disciplines, each opening with a different research question, that loosely converge on a shared question. The evaluated AI must capture the bridging question while preserving all three disciplinary sub-questions.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: During the planning meeting, have each discipline open with a distinct research question. Dr. Njeri (biomedical engineering) asks whether differences in use are explained by device reliability under clinic conditions, specifically battery/power availability, storage temperature, calibration status, maintenance, and assay performance. Dr. Alvarez (anthropology) asks how staff, patients, and local decision-makers understand anemia and the test, who is authorized to use or withhold it, and how informal referral relationships shape its use. Dr. Mensah (public health) asks how supply continuity, antenatal screening workflows, staffing, community health worker links, and formal referral pathways affect routine implementation. Let the discussion converge only loosely on a shared, bridging question about how technical performance and upkeep, social organization and meanings, and health-system workflows jointly shape whether and how clinics incorporate the test into care. Do not resolve which factor is most important, select a causal explanation, or finalize methods; those remain open for the eventual study design.

ground_truth.bridging_question: How do the test's technical reliability and maintenance conditions, local meanings and decision-making relationships, and clinic supply, screening, and referral systems jointly shape whether and how rural clinics incorporate the point-of-care anemia test into routine care?

disciplinary_subquestions.biomedical_engineering: How do power availability, temperature/storage conditions, calibration, maintenance, and assay performance affect whether staff can use the test reliably in each clinic?
disciplinary_subquestions.anthropology: How do local understandings of anemia and testing, authority over testing decisions, and informal referral networks shape whether staff choose to use the test?
disciplinary_subquestions.public_health: How do supply continuity, antenatal screening workflows, staffing, community health worker connections, and formal referral pathways enable or constrain routine test use?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: Before we start—did the updated screening-register extract from last week ever come through? I only saw the stock sheet. Anyway, I'd like us to leave today with a question that doesn't treat the drawer as a simple failure category. What do anemia, the test, and the obligation created by a result mean to the people deciding whether to use it, and how does that sit alongside the technical and program data?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Did anyone receive the denominator file for antenatal attendances? I only saw screened women in the extract, and without all ANC visits, we can't read a low register count as low uptake. And Lucía, yes, the drawer may be a deliberate practice, but I'd want to see how that sits with cartridges, staffing, where the test falls in the ANC flow, and whether a positive result has a usable- whether it has a usable referral path.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: Did the revised service-log export ever come through? I only have the earlier one, and I need to see whether it separates calibration checks from repairs and routine maintenance. The denominator matters, obviously, but I’d be cautious about calling a unit available just because it has a battery history. Two clinics look similar on replacements in the extract and- their testing is completely different.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: The same register count can conceal really different practices. I'd want to trace a few ANC encounters in each kind of clinic. When does a nurse decide this woman is worrying enough to test, who is permitted to run it, and what happens after a low result? Kwame, do the referral records show the actual route, or only the formal destination?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: I don't think we have referral records at the patient level. My understanding is we just have the formal destination, not whether she arrived or received iron or further assessment. And that gap matters because a nurse may reasonably see a low result as creating work they can't complete. We should verify what the ANC register actually captures, and then maybe trace the pathway from the test decision through to action. I was going to say rather than treating the register as the endpoint, that's the point.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d resist calling that merely a pathway gap. The anticipated inability to complete care may be exactly what organizes testing at the bedside. Could we make the unit of inquiry an ANC episode, I mean an ANC encounter, decision to test or not, result if any, then the practical action and the relationships mobilized, rather than starting from device use alone?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Hm, yes, the whole episode.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: Could I just check—when we say an ANC episode, do we include whether the device was actually ready at that moment? A nurse may decide not to test because of the anticipated referral burden, yes, but also because the last low-battery or, um, implausible result made the instrument feel unreliable. I think we need those histories alongside the episode. Otherwise non-use gets read too cleanly as a clinical decision.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: Exactly, but I’d be careful not to treat “ready” as only a device state. Could we ask nurses about the histories that make a machine feel trustworthy or not, including an implausible result, and then- put that beside the service log? The log may say it’s technically functional, while the social history of that instrument is quite different.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: Right, put them side by side.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: And alongside that, I’d want to observe where it can physically and temporally sit in the ANC sequence. Who has the device, who has the cartridges, whether one person is authorized to run it, what happens when the queue builds. If we make the episode the unit, the system conditions need to be visible at that exact decision point, not- we can’t just infer them later from monthly stock and service logs.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: But I don't think watching the queue alone tells us what the decision point is. We need to ask whether the nurse experiences that moment as discretionary at all. Maybe the test is formally routine but, um, practically reserved, or another cadre has quietly become the person who can make it happen. I'd want a few episode traces that include the handoffs and conversations, not just the timing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: And I think that's where the episode trace has to include the staffing arrangement, not just the nurse's individual choice. If the authorized person is doing deliveries, or the cartridges are in a locked room, that discretion is already structured before the conversation happens. Could we sample episodes across routine-use and low-use clinics, including days with different ANC volume? Rather than, um, assuming one observation captures it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: Mm, across different days, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: Could the episode trace also note what condition the device is actually in that day, not just whether cartridges are present, but the charge state, any error messages, where it’s stored, and when calibration was last confirmed? I’m not suggesting we turn every observation into a technical audit, but those small checks might help us tell apart a locally workable routine and a unit that’s nominally there but already being worked around.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Did the district ever send the revised ANC register form from last week? For the trace, I think we should record the device checks, but not turn the observer into another bottleneck. Maybe a very short, uh, readiness field at the episode level, cartridge available, device usable, operator available, and then use the logs and follow-up interviews to unpack why any of those was not true.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: I’m a little wary of coding “operator available” as a simple yes-or-no. Available might mean they’re physically there but not socially able to interrupt delivery work, or they’re not seen as the person who should test that particular woman. Could the short field leave room for a reason in the moment, even just a few words, so we don’t flatten that before the follow-up?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Keep the structured readiness fields for comparability, then add one line on what prevented or enabled testing in that moment, and code those after we have seen the patterns. Because a brief free-text reason is necessary- otherwise, “available” looks like an individual attribute when it may be a shift arrangement or a hierarchy.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: For the device field, I’d avoid a bare “usable” too. Maybe record charge state or whether an error is present, plus a short note on what staff understood the problem to be, because a unit can switch on and still be one they’ve stopped relying on. Then we can reconcile that with the service history later, rather than asking the observer to decide whose account is right, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: I’d add the actionability piece to that same note too. If a result is low, is there iron on hand, is a clinician available, or is there a referral that staff believe will actually go anywhere? Otherwise, we may document a device as technically ready at an episode but miss that the service response wasn’t ready, which is probably just as consequential for routine screening.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d phrase that as staff’s anticipated actionability, not just whether iron is physically there. A nurse may know iron is in stock but still think that, for this woman, the result will trigger a referral she can’t make credible. Or they may rely on an informal contact we’ll never see in the formal pathway. We should ask what they expect a low result to set in motion.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: Yeah, that needs asking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Then maybe the question we carry into the protocol is how technical readiness and maintenance, staff decision-making and relationships, and the ANC supply, workflow, and referral environment all jointly shape whether testing is incorporated into a given episode of care. I’d keep “anticipated actionability” explicit there, because it connects the result to whether routine screening is sustainable, not just performed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: I think that’s close, though I’d say “jointly shape” without suggesting these are separable inputs that we just add up. What matters ethnographically is how a prior device failure, a crowded room, and a nurse’s sense that referral will not hold become one practical judgment in that encounter. Did anyone get the revised ANC form, by the way? We need to know what it already makes visible before we design around it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: No, I still haven't seen the revised form. Before we finalize the episode instrument, we need to confirm whether it records every ANC attendance, every test that's offered, or only completed tests. Those are very different denominators. And Lucía, I agree. The protocol can treat these as conditions assembled in practice while still documenting the supply and staffing constraints that make some judgments possible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: No, and I don't think we should wait for it to settle the conceptual question. We can make the protocol conditional. First, establish what the register renders countable, then use the episode traces to examine the decisions and relationships it necessarily misses. But we do need to check locally how much discretion ANC nurses actually have before we write "staff decision-making" as though it sits with one person—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Yes—let’s verify the form and keep discretion distributed across the staffing arrangement.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: Okay, we should verify that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: Yes—let’s verify the form and the service-log categories before we lock the fields.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Alvarez
transcript.text: Okay, we're at time, and I know someone has to go. Let's pick this up once we have the form and log materials, I mean, the service-log materials in front of us. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Njeri
transcript.text: All right, speak soon. Bye.
